newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia rubber fund used up, not missing -ministe.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia rubber fund used up, not missing -ministe.

text.p: Malaysia's top commodities official said on Wednesday that a fund set up by the country for replanting rubber was used up and not misappropriated as alleged.
Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik denied any malpractices over the depleted fund of the Rubber Industry Smallholders Development Authority (RISDA).

But he said about 240 million ringgit ($95.3 million) was urgently required by RISDA to help rubber smallholders, who produce 85 percent of the country's annual one million tonnes of rubber, to upgrade their crops.
"I'd like to clarify that the RISDA replanting fund was used up and has not gone missing," Lim told a news conference.
"We have a rubber products and furniture industry worth 10 billion ringgit which depends wholly on rubber trees...so we must inject money into this fund immediately," he said.
Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim demanded an explanation from Lim after local newspapers quoted him as saying last week that some 600 million ringgit was missing from RISDA's replanting fund.
Annuar Musa, another minister responsible for RISDA, was also asked to explain.

Malaysia is cracking down on corruption in the government. The RISDA story caught the attention of acting Prime Minister Anwar during a week when at least 10 senior politicians were being investigated for possible graft.
Workers at RISDA on Wednesday demanded an apology from Lim for the confusion.

Lim said the "missing 600 million ringgit" was misinterpreted from a press statement he issued, in which he said the RISDA replanting fund should ideally be around 600 million ringgit but was empty instead.

"I have suggested to the Cabinet now that the 600 million be made into a revolving fund exclusively for replanting of rubber trees," said Lim. "The money can be either be raised through the privatisation of RISDA or injection of government funds."
Lim said the fund was until now made up of cess collected from rubber growers and exporters.
He said the cess has been 9.92 cents a kg since 1952, while the cost of replanting one hectare of rubber has swelled from 1,700 ringgit a hectare in 1952 to 6,000 ringgit.
"We have to replant at least 40,000 hectares a year but we only collect about 80 million ringgit in cess," said Lim.
He said rubber prices have been in the doldrums in recent years and unless an urgent solution was found, smallholders would become increasingly disillusioned about staying in the industry.
Malaysia has about 1.7 million hectares under rubber now, but was steadily losing 30,000 hectares a year to palm oil, the country's best-paying crop, said Lim.
